final.title: What bounced addresses are really telling you
final.body:
A bounced address is usually not the real problem. It is a symptom that something in the workflow is leaking: a typo at capture, stale CRM data, a bad import, or a contact list that nobody owns closely enough. For a small business owner, the real question is not “should we use AI?” It is whether this is a repeatable email and CRM cleanup problem, or just occasional noise that a person can clear faster than any system.

That distinction matters. If bounces happen often enough to block replies, create data debt, or leave follow-up stranded, there is a bounded workflow worth mapping. If they are rare, the fix may be simpler: better forms, a clearer list owner, or a manual review step. No need to send a robot into a room with one sticky note and call it strategy.

The practical next step is to take one week of bounced messages and trace each one back to its source. Note whether it came from a form, an import, a sales reply, or an old record. Then ask one question: does a human still need to decide what to retry, suppress, or investigate? If yes, that is a good sign the workflow is worth a controlled automation discussion. If no, you probably need cleaner input, not more tooling. Human approval stays on any list changes either way.
